title: Claude and ChatGPT Enter Protein Structure Prediction: General-Purpose Large Models Challenge AlphaFold's Specialist Status

content_html:
Xinming Tu, a researcher at the AI biotech company Phylo, used large models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google earlier this month to test their ability to predict little-known bacterial protein sequences. He let the analysis program run overnight, and the next day was very surprised by the results—Anthropic's latest version of Claude not only outperformed other large models, but also surpassed specialized tools trained on protein sequences. The finding, which he shared with Leo Chen of Harvard Medical School, sparked heated discussion in the computational biology community.

On Tuesday, OpenAI announced that its latest large model had successfully designed new proteins, and when synthesized and tested in the lab, some of the new proteins behaved as expected. The research sparked discussions about the future of biological AI, with some scientists predicting that general-purpose models like Claude and ChatGPT may surpass specialized tools such as AlphaFold in tasks such as protein structure prediction and design.

But some researchers have questioned this, arguing that some of the capabilities shown by large models may be merely mechanical repetition of training data, rather than true understanding or generalization. At the heart of the controversy is whether general-purpose large models have the potential to replace specialized tools in the highly specialized field of biological computing, or whether they are merely exhibiting surface-level capabilities on specific datasets.

If general-purpose models can indeed compete with or even surpass AlphaFold in protein structure prediction and design, it would mean that the capability boundary of large models is expanding from language and code to more fundamental scientific computing, and the paradigm for applying AI in the life sciences may change accordingly.
